output:
Dear Nana,

I hate that I can’t be there with you tomorrow night, sitting in the kitchen on Kathleen Street one last time before the move. I’m on call that whole week, and I tried to find someone to swap with me, but I couldn’t make it work. I’m sorry. I know you’ve told me it’s fine, and everyone else says it’s fine too. I’m trying to believe you all. But I still wish I could be there.

I’ve been trying to write this for a while. Every time I start, I get choked up and close the laptop. So I’m going to try to say it plainly: that house has meant an enormous amount to me, because you were there.

Fifty-one years on Kathleen Street. Half the family growing up in that kitchen. Grandpa Walt there, and then gone, and you carrying on. The house holds so many memories, but the reason they matter is you. I don’t want to make this sound like a funeral for the house. It isn’t. A house can be left behind without everything inside it being lost. We’ll take the stories with us—and, apparently, Denise will take the cuckoo clock and cedar chest. I’ve put my claim in for the crib board, so I feel like the important historical artifacts are in good hands.

Some of my favorite memories are the ordinary ones. Summer visits, the little TV in the kitchen, and you letting me stay up to watch the Expos or Jays as long as I dried the dishes. You taught me crib when I was about seven, and I’m fairly sure you never let me win once. When I finally skunked you at fifteen, you made me a whole pan of butter tarts. I still don’t know whether that was a reward, a peace offering, or a way to make sure I’d come back for another game. Probably all three.

I remember the back steps, too. You’d sit there with your tea at six in the morning, and I’d come out and sit with you. You never said much until you’d finished your cup. I didn’t understand then how nice it was to have someone beside you who didn’t need to fill every quiet moment. I understand now. I can still picture that morning light and your tea, and I’m grateful for all those quiet minutes.

When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me a twenty-dollar bill taped inside a card. “For pizza, you look thin on the computer.” That’s still one of the best things anyone has ever said to me. You managed to worry about me, feed me, and make me laugh all in one sentence.

And I still laugh about last Christmas, when my pager went off during dinner and you asked if the internet was broken again and if I’d fixed it. Now every time I call, you ask, “Did anything break?” Nana, if the answer were ever “no,” I’m not sure I’d know what to do with myself.

I want you to know how proud I am of you. You chose Elmwood Terrace yourself. Nobody made you go. You looked at what was ahead, decided what you wanted, and picked a place that actually looks nice—and has a crib league. I mean, a retirement place with crib? You’ve basically found a new competitor pool. I’ll try not to be intimidated.

I know moving out of a home you’ve lived in for 51 years is a big thing, even when you’re ready for what comes next. I hope you’re excited. I hope you like having people around, and that the maple outside your room turns out to be a good one to watch through the seasons. The parking lot may not sound like the world’s most romantic view, but a big maple can do a lot of heavy lifting. And on the second floor, you’ll have a good vantage point for keeping an eye on things.

I wish I could be there tomorrow to sit in that kitchen with you. I can’t change the call schedule, and I’m sorry it worked out this way. But I don’t want you to mistake my absence for not caring. I care a lot. That house meant so much to me, and so did every summer, every game, every cup of tea, every butter tart, and every time you checked whether I’d eaten enough.

I’ll come up the weekend of December 5, once this rotation is done. I’ll bring the crib board, and we’ll play our first game at Elmwood. I’m not going to ask you to let me win. I know better by now. But if I happen to skunk you again, I’ll consider it a family tradition if you make me butter tarts.

I love you, Nana. I hope tomorrow night feels like a goodbye to a house you loved, not a goodbye to the life you made there. That life is coming with you. And I can’t wait to sit down across from you in the new place, shuffle the cards, and hear you ask if anything broke.

Love,

[Your name]
